title: Officer was forced to shoot, inquest told
article: The senior police officer who fired the shots that ultimately ended the life of a mentally ill man high on cocaine said it might have ended differently if he had been able to quickly flee the man's small trailer.
But Cpl. Greg Pask stands by his decision to pull the trigger.

"The ideal situation would have been to exit the trailer," he told a four-man, three-woman jury and presiding coroner Rodrick MacKenzie during the first day of an expected four-day inquest into the March 1, 2009 death of Derek Wayne Welton.

The inquest's aim is to publicly assess the facts, to make recommendations, which may help prevent the loss of life in the future, and to satisfy the community that circumstances were not overlooked or ignored, said MacKenzie.
A call from Welton's mobile phone prompted a quick but careful response to the incident from North Cowichan/ Duncan RCMP that spring evening.
"This is war dog flight squadron leader and I comply, you must get my flight squadron airborne now," the voice on the phone said, adding police protection was needed.
In multiple 9-1-1 calls, Welton told dispatch, "So many people have died over the lies of BC Hydro," and he'd "gone to hell and back."
Welton also told dispatchers he was scared, that he hadn't done anything wrong, and that the police had beaten him up "so many times" and that he didn't feel safe.
"I am going to arm myself and they are going to have to \[expletive\] shoot me," he told dispatch, refusing to leave his trailer.

Police didn't know Welton was released from a forensic psychiatric hospital just two months before, but from past encounters they knew he was a mentally unstable and often violent cocaine user with a particular disdain for law enforcement.
That's why multiple officers and a police service dog mustered outside the Duncan RV Park on Boys Road around 5:50 p.m. before approaching Welton's trailer.
"The more the merrier if we have to do something," the jury heard Const. Greg Bouvier tell fellow officers on a recording of police radio communications.
Bouvier later explained he'd had a previous run-in with Welton where Welton punched him three times in the face before instigating a ground fight requiring four officers to subdue him.
"He fights through Tasers and OC (pepper) spray," Bouvier explained. "Derek wasn't a big man. He was tall and lean but when he's high on drugs...or mentally ill, he's a force to be reckoned with."
With the risk of violence high, officers had initially planned to calm Welton down enough for him to freely exit his trailer and be taken to hospital for treatment under the Mental Health Act.
The ambulance was standing by to make the transfer but it didn't go as planned.
Pask, the day shift watch commander, had dealt with Welton before and was called in when the agitated man asked to speak with a supervisor.
Pask calmed Welton enough to get him to unlock the trailer door but Welton wouldn't come out.
Pask went in instead, backed by Const. Kara Gelech and night shift watch commander Cpl. Bob Purslow.
After a short conversation, Welton's level of agitation was again increasing. Gelech deployed her Taser and Pask went in to handcuff the man. But he didn't get far.

"When I saw him grab for the knives it became apparent to me that the Taser was not having the desired effect," Pask said. "I just remember him standing up and grabbing a knife and bringing it up and coming towards me."
The officer backed toward the door but with Gelech and Purslow in the entryway behind him, and Bouvier just outside the door, Pask was trapped. That's when he fired the first shot.
"It did not appear to have any effect at all," said the officer, noting he attempted to leave the trailer after but the only doorway was still blocked.
Pask shot a second time and "he \[Welton\] appeared for a brief millisecond, to be stung by it."
Again Pask attempted to retreat but the other officers were still on their way out ahead of him.
Pask said he fired a third shot before he was able to retreat.
"He was still attacking me with the knife," he explained.
Const. Garfield Henderson, Bouvier and Purslow then entered the trailer to arrest Welton and address his injuries.
It was later learned that two of the three bullets struck Welton, but true to his history, he'd kept fighting.

"I couldn't believe he'd just been shot and...he was throwing (Bouvier and Purslow) around like rag dolls," Henderson said. "For five or 10 seconds it was absolute chaos. We were fighting for our lives."
Henderson said he was surprised to hear Welton died in hospital a short time later.

Christine Dagenais, a forensic toxicology specialist, told the inquest Tuesday that Welton had smoked cocaine three to five hours prior to his death and had also used marijuana that day. He had been prescribed anti-psychotic medication, but none was found in his system.

Entrance and exit strategies were not discussed prior to three officers entering Welton's small trailer because it would have been "impractical" said Pask, noting going in alone was not an option given the safety risk it posed.
"It's difficult for us to anticipate what's going to happen and know how the situation is going to play out," he said.
It would have been "something to consider" moving forward, Pask added. "You really have to take it case by case."
The inquest is expected to wrap up by week's end.
